result.markdown: --- title: "09 · Model selection" subtitle: "Week 3" --- ::: {.guiding-q} How do I select the best model? ::: ## In this session - What "best" means: testing hypotheses vs. predicting well - Full–null model comparisons and likelihood-ratio tests - Information criteria (AIC) and multi-model inference - Overfitting, and why stepwise selection is a problem - Pre-specifying the model as the default for confirmatory analyses ::: {.key-terms} **Key terms:** [AIC (Akaike information criterion)](../../glossary.qmd#aic), [Likelihood-ratio test](../../glossary.qmd#lrt), [Full–null model comparison](../../glossary.qmd#full-null), [Overfitting](../../glossary.qmd#overfitting), [Model selection](../../glossary.qmd#model-selection) ::: ## Learning goals After this session you can - compare nested models with a likelihood-ratio test, - use and interpret AIC for a set of candidate models, - explain why selecting predictors by *p*-values inflates false positives. ## Simulate first Adding predictors that are pure noise always increases R². A good model selection strategy must guard against this. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(9) n <- 40 noise <- as.data.frame(matrix(rnorm(n * 20), n)) y <- rnorm(n) # y is unrelated to all predictors r2 <- sapply(1:20, function(k) summary(lm(y ~ ., data = noise[, 1:k, drop = FALSE]))$r.squared) plot(1:20, r2, type = "b", pch = 19, col = "#c0392b", xlab = "Number of noise predictors", ylab = expression(R^2)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](09-model-selection_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-1-1.png){width=975} ::: ::: ## Materials ::: {.materials} - Slides coming soon - R script coming soon - Exercises coming soon ::: ## Reading - Burnham, K. P., & Anderson, D. R. (2002). *Model selection and multimodel inference* (2nd ed.). Springer. - Forstmeier, W., & Schielzeth, H. (2011). Cryptic multiple hypotheses testing in linear models: Overestimated effect sizes and the winner's curse. *Behavioral Ecology and Sociobiology, 65*, 47–55.
